transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi Doc. I guess... I mean, they told me I needed to come see somebody because, well, what brings me in is I just hardly eat right anymore. I don't know what it is, it's like my stomach just shut down on me or my brain completely forgot how to be hungry. 

Some days, and I mean a whole lot of days lately, it is just coffee. I'll make a pot in the morning and just sit there drinking that, and maybe, if I really force myself because I know a person is supposed to eat something, I'll have a piece of bread. Just a plain piece of bread, no butter or meat or nothing on it, just folding it up and chewing it like it's cardboard just so I have something in my belly. 

And it's really starting to show, you know? Like, my pants are just hanging loose on me now. I put on my regular jeans the other day, the ones that used to fit me just fine, and they practically slid right down my hips. I had to dig around in my room to find this old belt I haven't worn in years, and I had to pull it so tight that the fabric gets all bunched up and looks ridiculous. I just look hollowed out, but I can't bring myself to sit down for a real meal. It's just the coffee and that bread, day after day, and I'm just shrinking out of my own clothes.
When you think about eating more, do you feel afraid that it might make you gain weight or change your body, or is it more that you just don't feel hungry or interested in food at all?

Nah, no, it ain't nothing like that at all. I ain't scared of getting fat or nothing. Honestly, I'd give just about anything to put some meat back on my bones, 'cause like I said, I'm looking all hollowed out and sick, and I don't like looking like this. I look in the mirror and I don't even hardly recognize my own face with my cheeks all sunk in. So it ain't about my weight, I ain't trying to be on no diet. 

It's just... I look at food, even stuff I used to really like, you know? Like, I used to could put away a whole double cheeseburger and fries, no problem, maybe even go back for seconds if I was busy doing stuff all day. But now? Now I just look at a plate and my stomach just completely turns over. It's like my mouth forgets what to do with it. 

Just the other day, my buddy brought over some fried chicken, trying to be nice, you know, saying "you gotta eat, man, you're fading away." And I took a piece, mostly just to get him off my back so he'd quit looking at me like I was a dying dog, and I bit into it... and I swear to you Doc, it felt like I was chewing on a wad of dry cotton. I just kept chewing and chewing and my throat just closed up. I couldn't even swallow it down. I had to pretend to wipe my mouth and spit it out in a paper towel when he turned around to look at the TV. 

So it ain't that I'm trying to be skinny or scared of the scale or none of that. My brain just... it just don't want it. It's like the switch for being hungry just got flipped all the way off and somebody broke the handle off so I can't flip it back on. I just don't care about food no more. I don't even think about it until my stomach actually starts cramping up, and even then, I just pour another cup of that black coffee to make the cramping stop because the thought of actually swallowing a meal just sounds like a chore I ain't got the energy for.
Over these past weeks, have you also been feeling down, sad, or empty most of the day, or have you lost interest and pleasure in things you normally enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, I guess that's exactly what it is. It's... well, most days, I open my eyes, right? And before I even move, before I even think about swinging my legs over the side of the mattress, it just hits me. It's this... this real heavy, empty feeling right here in the middle of my chest. It ain't like a physical pain, not like a heart attack or nothing, it's just... heavy. Like somebody snuck in while I was sleeping and parked a cinderblock right on my ribs. 

And I just lay there staring up at the ceiling, looking at this old water stain up there, and I just think, what is even the point of getting up? There ain't nothing good waiting for me out there. Not a single good thing. It's just another day of absolutely nothing. I used to at least want to get up and, I don't know, maybe go sit out on the porch or tinker with some junk in the yard, watch the cars go by. But now... now I just lay there with that weight on my chest, feeling completely hollowed out on the inside. 

I just want to pull that old quilt right back up over my face and keep my head down. Just keep my head down and hide away from the whole world, you know? It's like the color just got completely sucked out of everything. I don't want to talk to nobody, I don't want to see nobody. Like when my buddy brought that chicken over, I was just wishing he'd leave the whole time so I could go back to just sitting in the quiet. It's just this constant, dragging emptiness that won't let up. It's there in the morning, it's there when I'm choking down that black coffee, and it's still sitting right there on my chest when the sun finally goes down. I just feel completely empty, Doc. Like a dried-up well that ain't got nothing left to give.
Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks or months where you felt this same kind of deep sadness, emptiness, and loss of interest—at any earlier point in your life?

Well, see, that's the thing. I've been trying to think back on that, trying to figure out if I've always been this way or if this is just... just how it is now. And to be honest with you, Doc, it feels like this particular spell, this exact heavy, empty feeling... it's been hanging over me for about five months now. 

I remember because it started right around the time the leaves started turning brown and falling off the trees in the yard. I remember looking out the window one morning, holding my coffee, and seeing the yard just covered in dead leaves, and I thought to myself, "I need to get out there and rake those up." But I didn't. I just stood there looking at them, and that heavy feeling just sort of settled right into my chest, right then and there. And the leaves just stayed there. They got all wet and matted down from the rain, and then the snow covered them up, and now the snow's melting and they're still there, just a rotting mess. 

And that's exactly how long this has been going on. Five whole months of just... nothing. Five months of waking up and feeling like I'm already exhausted before I even put my feet on the floor. I mean, maybe I had days before where I felt a little down, you know, like everybody gets the blues sometimes if something bad happens or whatever. But nothing like this. Not this... not this constant, five-month stretch where every single day is exactly the same shade of gray. 

It's like I crossed a line back in the fall and I haven't been able to find my way back since. I keep thinking maybe tomorrow I'll wake up and the cinderblock won't be there, but it always is. Every morning for five months, regular as a clock. I just lay there and think about those rotting leaves in the yard and how I ain't got the strength to do a single thing about them, or about anything else for that matter. It's just been this one, long, unbroken stretch of feeling completely dried up inside since way back then.
During these past five months, have you had any thoughts of wanting to hurt yourself or that you'd be better off not being alive?

No, no, I ain't... I ain't had no thoughts like that. I know it probably sounds like I would, what with me telling you how I just lay there all day feeling like a dried-up well and all, but no. I ain't sitting in that bed thinking about hurting myself or wishing I was dead. 

Truth be told, Doc, doing something like that... well, that takes a whole lot of effort, don't it? It takes energy to plan something out, to actually get up and do some harm to yourself, and like I said, I ain't even got the energy to chew a piece of chicken or rake them rotting leaves out front. So the thought of actually doing something to myself? My brain don't even go there. It's just too much work. 

And as for being better off not being alive... I don't really think about being dead. I just think about how exhausted I am being awake. It's like... I remember when I was a kid, my granddaddy had this old hound dog, Buster. Buster got real old and his hips gave out, and he'd just lay on the porch all day. He wasn't trying to die, he wasn't doing nothing to hurt himself, he was just... done with running around. He just wanted to lay there and be left alone. That's kind of how my brain is right now. I ain't looking to end it all or check out for good. I don't want to die. I just... I just don't want to have to *do* anything, you know? 

I just want to lay there under that quilt and not have to face the day or feel that cinderblock on my chest. I just wish time would pause for a while so I could catch my breath. But no, I ain't never thought about taking a knife or a pill or doing nothing crazy like that. I just lay there, stare at that water stain, and wait for the sun to go down again. That's all I do.
Over these past five months, how has your sleep been—are you having trouble falling or staying asleep, or are you sleeping much more than usual?

Sleep... man, sleep is a whole other mess. It's like my body is just so tired, so heavy, but when I actually get in that bed, it all just falls apart. I pull that old quilt up, hoping I can just shut my eyes and make the whole world disappear for a while, but it don't work like that no more. 

Lately, I just end up lying there for hours. Just staring right at the wall. There's this one spot on the drywall right next to the bed where the paint's sort of bubbling up, kind of looks like a little map of Texas if you squint at it, and I just stare at it. Hours go by. The house gets real quiet, you hear every little creak and groan in the floorboards, you hear the wind outside, and I'm just laying there, wide awake, with that cinderblock sitting right on my chest. I try rolling over, try closing my eyes real tight, but nothing happens. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off... it ain't for long. I'll just suddenly wake up, and it's pitch black outside. The sun ain't even thought about coming up yet. It'll be, I don't know, three or four in the morning, dead quiet, and that's it. Sleep's done. I try to force it, I tell myself, "Just go back to sleep, ain't nothing to get up for anyway," but I absolutely cannot get back to sleep. I just lay there listening to the dark, waiting for the light to finally start creeping in through the blinds, which takes forever. 

But I think the worst part of it all, Doc, is that even when I *do* manage to get a few hours of sleep in, it don't do me no good. It ain't restful at all. When the morning finally comes, I feel completely worn out. I wake up feeling just as exhausted as I did when I laid down. It's like I've been out digging ditches all night long in my sleep. My body just feels totally drained, no matter if my eyes were closed or not. It's just a miserable way to spend the night, every single night, just staring at that peeling paint on the wall and feeling so damn tired but not being able to actually get a single minute of real rest.

Over these past five months, has this been affecting your ability to keep up with basic day-to-day responsibilities, like managing your household, going to work, or taking care of things you're normally responsible for?

Well, Doc, to put it plain, everything has just completely gone to seed. I mean, you remember me telling you about them leaves in the yard just sitting there rotting, right? Well, the inside of the house ain't looking much better, and my actual life is about in the same shape. I just ain't keeping up with nothing. Not a single thing. Basic errands, the kind of stuff a person normally doesn't even think twice about, like running down to the store for a gallon of milk or some dish soap or taking the trash to the dump? I just can't do it. I look at my truck keys sitting there on the kitchen counter and it feels like they weigh a hundred pounds. I am just not keeping up with basic errands the way I used to, not by a long shot.

Since this whole thing got real bad back in the fall, I have had to lean on my relatives for pretty much everything, and I hate being a burden, I really do, but I ain't got a choice. I ain't working right now, ain't been in the workforce for a bit, so the money situation was already tight, but now my folks are having to step in and help me out with money just to make sure the electric bill gets paid and I don't end up sitting in the dark freezing. 

And even if I had the cash in my pocket, I ain't driving nowhere. I just don't trust my brain behind the wheel feeling this exhausted and heavy all the time, so my sister or my uncle, they have to come give me rides if I absolutely have to be somewhere, like coming down here to the clinic to see you today. If they don't drive me, I just don't go. 

And the paperwork... Lord, don't even get me started on the paperwork. The mail just piles up on the kitchen table. Envelopes with red letters, bills, forms, all that official stuff. Now, I will be straight with you, I never was much for school, didn't even make it to the ninth grade, so reading through all that official mumbo-jumbo was always a real heavy chore for me anyway. But now? With my head feeling like it is stuffed full of wet cotton? Looking at them papers is like trying to read Greek. My brain just scrambles it all up and I get so overwhelmed I just want to put my head down on the table and cry. So my sister, she has been coming over once a week to sort through that mountain of mail, handling all the paperwork for me, telling me where to sign, making sure the county don't come after me or nothing. If it wasn't for my relatives stepping in to help with the money, the rides, and all them forms, I don't even know where I would be right now. I am just completely useless when it comes to taking care of my own day-to-day life anymore.
Have others, like your sister or your buddy, mentioned noticing you moving or talking more slowly than usual, or seeming restless and fidgety, over these past few months?

Yeah, they sure have. My sister, she was just saying the other day... well, she tries to be patient with me, she really does, but I know it wears on her. She tells me I move like I am walking through mud. Thick, heavy mud. And honestly, Doc, that's exactly what it feels like. It's like I got lead weights tied to my boots and every single step is just a massive effort. I'll just be trying to shuffle from the bedroom to the kitchen sink for a glass of water, and it takes me forever. I just drag my feet across the linoleum. It ain't that I'm trying to be slow, it's just... the signal from my brain to my legs is just stuck in molasses or something. I ain't fidgety at all, no sir. I ain't got the energy to be bouncing my knee or pacing around. I'm just practically standing still most of the time. 

And the talking part... man, that's almost worse. My family says sometimes it takes me a long time to answer even a simple question. And they ain't wrong. My sister will ask me something real basic, like, "Hey, did you eat that sandwich I left in the fridge?" or "Do you want me to leave the hall light on?" Just simple stuff you shouldn't even have to think about. But I'll just sit there, staring at her. I hear the words, I know what she's asking me, but my brain just can't seem to find the gear to answer back. It's like the words get stuck somewhere between my head and my mouth. I have to really, really concentrate just to push a "yes" or a "no" out. 

My buddy came over Tuesday to check on me, asked if I wanted him to open a window to let some fresh air in, and I swear it must have been a full minute of me just looking at him blankly before I could even manage to nod my head. I just couldn't process it fast enough to speak. Everything about me is just dialed down to an absolute crawl right now. It's just frustrating for them to have to stand there and wait on me, and it's frustrating for me to feel so... broken down.

doctor.intent: Determine whether this is a first depressive episode or part of a recurrent pattern, to distinguish single-episode from recurrent major depressive disorder
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period like this before—weeks or months where you felt this same kind of deep sadness, emptiness, and loss of interest—at any earlier point in your life?

target_item.name: Depressive Episode Duration
target_item.manifestation: This depressed spell has been hanging over me for about five months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the history and timeline of the depressive symptoms. The patient's profile specifies the duration of the current depressive episode, which is the most relevant information to address the timeline of these feelings.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that's the thing. I've been trying to think back on that, trying to figure out if I've always been this way or if this is just... just how it is now. And to be honest with you, Doc, it feels like this particular spell, this exact heavy, empty feeling... it's been hanging over me for about five months now. 

I remember because it started right around the time the leaves started turning brown and falling off the trees in the yard. I remember looking out the window one morning, holding my coffee, and seeing the yard just covered in dead leaves, and I thought to myself, "I need to get out there and rake those up." But I didn't. I just stood there looking at them, and that heavy feeling just sort of settled right into my chest, right then and there. And the leaves just stayed there. They got all wet and matted down from the rain, and then the snow covered them up, and now the snow's melting and they're still there, just a rotting mess. 

And that's exactly how long this has been going on. Five whole months of just... nothing. Five months of waking up and feeling like I'm already exhausted before I even put my feet on the floor. I mean, maybe I had days before where I felt a little down, you know, like everybody gets the blues sometimes if something bad happens or whatever. But nothing like this. Not this... not this constant, five-month stretch where every single day is exactly the same shade of gray. 

It's like I crossed a line back in the fall and I haven't been able to find my way back since. I keep thinking maybe tomorrow I'll wake up and the cinderblock won't be there, but it always is. Every morning for five months, regular as a clock. I just lay there and think about those rotting leaves in the yard and how I ain't got the strength to do a single thing about them, or about anything else for that matter. It's just been this one, long, unbroken stretch of feeling completely dried up inside since way back then.

inference.note: Patient denies any prior episodes of this severity, describing this as a single unbroken 5-month stretch, which rules out recurrent depressive disorder (F33.9). Symptoms consistent with a single major depressive episode with significant appetite loss and weight loss, without body image distortion or fear of weight gain, ruling out an eating disorder.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, which is critical for safety and diagnostic severity
doctor.question: During these past five months, have you had any thoughts of wanting to hurt yourself or that you'd be better off not being alive?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is not covered by any of the available symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
No, no, I ain't... I ain't had no thoughts like that. I know it probably sounds like I would, what with me telling you how I just lay there all day feeling like a dried-up well and all, but no. I ain't sitting in that bed thinking about hurting myself or wishing I was dead. 

Truth be told, Doc, doing something like that... well, that takes a whole lot of effort, don't it? It takes energy to plan something out, to actually get up and do some harm to yourself, and like I said, I ain't even got the energy to chew a piece of chicken or rake them rotting leaves out front. So the thought of actually doing something to myself? My brain don't even go there. It's just too much work. 

And as for being better off not being alive... I don't really think about being dead. I just think about how exhausted I am being awake. It's like... I remember when I was a kid, my granddaddy had this old hound dog, Buster. Buster got real old and his hips gave out, and he'd just lay on the porch all day. He wasn't trying to die, he wasn't doing nothing to hurt himself, he was just... done with running around. He just wanted to lay there and be left alone. That's kind of how my brain is right now. I ain't looking to end it all or check out for good. I don't want to die. I just... I just don't want to have to *do* anything, you know? 

I just want to lay there under that quilt and not have to face the day or feel that cinderblock on my chest. I just wish time would pause for a while so I could catch my breath. But no, I ain't never thought about taking a knife or a pill or doing nothing crazy like that. I just lay there, stare at that water stain, and wait for the sun to go down again. That's all I do.

inference.note: Five-month duration confirms this is a single depressive episode rather than recurrent; no prior similar episodes reported, ruling out F33. No suicidal ideation noted. Anorexia is appetite loss without body image distortion or fear of weight gain, ruling out eating disorders (F50.x). Symptoms remain consistent with major depressive disorder, single episode. Severity specifier still needs clarification (moderate vs severe) but F32.9 remains appropriate pending further detail.

doctor.intent: Assess for sleep disturbance (insomnia or hypersomnia), a core depressive symptom not yet explored
doctor.question: Over these past five months, how has your sleep been—are you having trouble falling or staying asleep, or are you sleeping much more than usual?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Lately I either lie there for hours staring at the wall or wake up before the sun and cannot get back to sleep, and even when I do sleep I feel worn out.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in my sleep patterns over the past five months, which directly corresponds to the sleep disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
Sleep... man, sleep is a whole other mess. It's like my body is just so tired, so heavy, but when I actually get in that bed, it all just falls apart. I pull that old quilt up, hoping I can just shut my eyes and make the whole world disappear for a while, but it don't work like that no more. 

Lately, I just end up lying there for hours. Just staring right at the wall. There's this one spot on the drywall right next to the bed where the paint's sort of bubbling up, kind of looks like a little map of Texas if you squint at it, and I just stare at it. Hours go by. The house gets real quiet, you hear every little creak and groan in the floorboards, you hear the wind outside, and I'm just laying there, wide awake, with that cinderblock sitting right on my chest. I try rolling over, try closing my eyes real tight, but nothing happens. 

And then, if I do finally manage to drift off... it ain't for long. I'll just suddenly wake up, and it's pitch black outside. The sun ain't even thought about coming up yet. It'll be, I don't know, three or four in the morning, dead quiet, and that's it. Sleep's done. I try to force it, I tell myself, "Just go back to sleep, ain't nothing to get up for anyway," but I absolutely cannot get back to sleep. I just lay there listening to the dark, waiting for the light to finally start creeping in through the blinds, which takes forever. 

But I think the worst part of it all, Doc, is that even when I *do* manage to get a few hours of sleep in, it don't do me no good. It ain't restful at all. When the morning finally comes, I feel completely worn out. I wake up feeling just as exhausted as I did when I laid down. It's like I've been out digging ditches all night long in my sleep. My body just feels totally drained, no matter if my eyes were closed or not. It's just a miserable way to spend the night, every single night, just staring at that peeling paint on the wall and feeling so damn tired but not being able to actually get a single minute of real rest.

inference.note: Symptoms now show clear melancholic depressive features (anhedonia, significant appetite/weight loss without body-image concerns, early morning awakening, non-restorative sleep, profound fatigue) sustained for 5 months, favoring a specific severity level (moderate-severe single episode) over the unspecified code; ruled out atypical/psychotic features and eating disorder due to lack of body image disturbance.

doctor.intent: Assess severity/functional impairment to distinguish moderate (F32.1) from severe (F32.2) depressive episode - specifically whether he can still manage basic daily functioning
doctor.question: Over these past five months, has this been affecting your ability to keep up with basic day-to-day responsibilities, like managing your household, going to work, or taking care of things you're normally responsible for?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: Since this got bad, I have needed my relatives to help with money, rides, and paperwork, and I am not keeping up with basic errands the way I used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my ability to keep up with day-to-day responsibilities, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, Doc, to put it plain, everything has just completely gone to seed. I mean, you remember me telling you about them leaves in the yard just sitting there rotting, right? Well, the inside of the house ain't looking much better, and my actual life is about in the same shape. I just ain't keeping up with nothing. Not a single thing. Basic errands, the kind of stuff a person normally doesn't even think twice about, like running down to the store for a gallon of milk or some dish soap or taking the trash to the dump? I just can't do it. I look at my truck keys sitting there on the kitchen counter and it feels like they weigh a hundred pounds. I am just not keeping up with basic errands the way I used to, not by a long shot.

Since this whole thing got real bad back in the fall, I have had to lean on my relatives for pretty much everything, and I hate being a burden, I really do, but I ain't got a choice. I ain't working right now, ain't been in the workforce for a bit, so the money situation was already tight, but now my folks are having to step in and help me out with money just to make sure the electric bill gets paid and I don't end up sitting in the dark freezing. 

And even if I had the cash in my pocket, I ain't driving nowhere. I just don't trust my brain behind the wheel feeling this exhausted and heavy all the time, so my sister or my uncle, they have to come give me rides if I absolutely have to be somewhere, like coming down here to the clinic to see you today. If they don't drive me, I just don't go. 

And the paperwork... Lord, don't even get me started on the paperwork. The mail just piles up on the kitchen table. Envelopes with red letters, bills, forms, all that official stuff. Now, I will be straight with you, I never was much for school, didn't even make it to the ninth grade, so reading through all that official mumbo-jumbo was always a real heavy chore for me anyway. But now? With my head feeling like it is stuffed full of wet cotton? Looking at them papers is like trying to read Greek. My brain just scrambles it all up and I get so overwhelmed I just want to put my head down on the table and cry. So my sister, she has been coming over once a week to sort through that mountain of mail, handling all the paperwork for me, telling me where to sign, making sure the county don't come after me or nothing. If it wasn't for my relatives stepping in to help with the money, the rides, and all them forms, I don't even know where I would be right now. I am just completely useless when it comes to taking care of my own day-to-day life anymore.

inference.note: The severe functional impairment (complete inability to manage household, finances, transportation, and paperwork), marked weight loss from food aversion, early morning awakening, non-restorative sleep, and pervasive anhedonia over 5 months are consistent with a single severe depressive episode without psychotic features, ruling out F32.1 (moderate) given the degree of functional incapacitation. No psychotic symptoms (hallucinations/delusions) reported, and no suicidal ideation, supporting F32.2 over F32.3.

doctor.intent: Assess psychomotor agitation or retardation observable to others, to satisfy another criterion for major depressive episode
doctor.question: Have others, like your sister or your buddy, mentioned noticing you moving or talking more slowly than usual, or seeming restless and fidgety, over these past few months?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My family says I move like I am walking through mud, and sometimes it takes me a long time to answer even a simple question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about observable changes in my movements or speech speed, such as moving or talking more slowly, which corresponds to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Yeah, they sure have. My sister, she was just saying the other day... well, she tries to be patient with me, she really does, but I know it wears on her. She tells me I move like I am walking through mud. Thick, heavy mud. And honestly, Doc, that's exactly what it feels like. It's like I got lead weights tied to my boots and every single step is just a massive effort. I'll just be trying to shuffle from the bedroom to the kitchen sink for a glass of water, and it takes me forever. I just drag my feet across the linoleum. It ain't that I'm trying to be slow, it's just... the signal from my brain to my legs is just stuck in molasses or something. I ain't fidgety at all, no sir. I ain't got the energy to be bouncing my knee or pacing around. I'm just practically standing still most of the time. 

And the talking part... man, that's almost worse. My family says sometimes it takes me a long time to answer even a simple question. And they ain't wrong. My sister will ask me something real basic, like, "Hey, did you eat that sandwich I left in the fridge?" or "Do you want me to leave the hall light on?" Just simple stuff you shouldn't even have to think about. But I'll just sit there, staring at her. I hear the words, I know what she's asking me, but my brain just can't seem to find the gear to answer back. It's like the words get stuck somewhere between my head and my mouth. I have to really, really concentrate just to push a "yes" or a "no" out. 

My buddy came over Tuesday to check on me, asked if I wanted him to open a window to let some fresh air in, and I swear it must have been a full minute of me just looking at him blankly before I could even manage to nod my head. I just couldn't process it fast enough to speak. Everything about me is just dialed down to an absolute crawl right now. It's just frustrating for them to have to stand there and wait on me, and it's frustrating for me to feel so... broken down.

inference.note: Psychomotor retardation, terminal insomnia, non-reactive mood, appetite/weight loss without body image disturbance, and marked functional impairment over 5 months confirm a single severe depressive episode with melancholic features. No prior manic/hypomanic or depressive episodes reported, ruling out recurrent depressive disorder (F33.x) or bipolar spectrum; no psychotic features noted, ruling out F32.3. Eating disturbance appears fully secondary to depression rather than a primary eating disorder, so no separate ARFID/anorexia code is needed.

opening_question.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit today
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a single, continuous 5-month episode of depressed mood, anhedonia, significant unintentional weight loss/appetite loss without body image disturbance or fear of weight gain (ruling out an eating disorder), insomnia with early morning awakening and non-restorative sleep, psychomotor retardation observed by others (slowed movement and speech latency), fatigue/loss of energy, and marked functional impairment requiring family assistance with finances, transportation, and household tasks. No prior manic/hypomanic or depressive episodes reported, and no suicidal ideation, psychotic features, or mood-incongruent symptoms. Severity of vegetative and psychomotor symptoms plus profound functional impairment supports severe (not moderate) major depressive episode without psychotic features.
